newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. praises Colombia drug law, quiet on sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. praises Colombia drug law, quiet on sanctions.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette praised Colombia on Saturday for passing tough new laws aimed at bankrupting billionaire drug barons.

He said the United States welcomed the asset forfeiture law, but did not say whether the new law could help avert the threat of U.S. economic sanctions against Colombia for its perceived failure to crack down on drug trafficking.
Colombia's congress on Thursday overwhelmingly approved the retroactive seizure of property and assets accumulated by the country's billionaire drug barons over the past 20 years.

"This (law) is a very important step. Excellent for Colombia in the fight against drugs. It will be a step recognised by my country and in the rest of the world," the Caracol radio network quoted Frechette as saying on Saturday. Frechette made the comments to the radio station as he arrived back in Bogota from Miami.

After five months of heated debate in congress -- during which time death threats and bribe offers were alleged to have been made by the jailed heads of the once powerful Cali drug cartel -- the asset forfeiture law seemed to be on the brink of collapse earlier this week.

The lower house of congress had voted down the provision allowing the government to seize drug barons' ill-gotten gains amassed over the last 20 years, ruling instead that only illicit fortunes accumulated since 1991 could be targeted.

President Ernesto Samper -- accused by Washington of having ties to drug cartels -- and other senior ministers lobbied lawmakers and pressured congress to reconsider the vote. In less than 48 hours, the government transformed what would have been a humiliating blow to its anti-drug efforts into an overwhelming victory. The lower house passed the measure by 103-4.

Political analysts said the measure alone was unlikely to lead to Colombia regaining certification as a U.S. ally in the drug war. The United States decertified Colombia last March amid allegations Samper used cash from the Cali cartel's cocaine trafficking to finance his 1994 election campaign, and threatened economic sanctions.

Buoyed by the success of Thursday night's vote, Samper said on Saturday that congress would hold an extraordinary session starting on Tuesday to consider a bill to introduce stiffer prison terms for drug traffickers.
